steelman: Temperature-0 LLM inference is reproducible in principle: the bit-level variation people observe is not an inescapable consequence of GPU floating-point arithmetic but an artifact of a specific engineering decision, namely that serving kernels for matmul, RMSNorm, and attention reduce over a batch whose composition and size shift with concurrent load, and floating-point addition is non-associative, so the same prompt lands in a different batch shape and accumulates in a different order. The proof is mechanistic, not merely correlational: at temperature 0, Qwen3-235B produced 80 distinct completions across 1000 runs, and swapping in batch-invariant kernels collapsed all 1000 to one identical output, isolating batch-variant reduction order as the cause [s1]. That determinism is purchasable at a known, bounded price (about 2x, 55s vs 26s, narrowing to 1.6x at 42s with better attention kernels) [s1], and the price need not be paid globally: a system like LLM-42 keeps a fast non-deterministic path and pays the determinism tax only on the traffic that demands it via a verify-rollback loop reusing existing kernels [s2]. The non-trivial claim is causal and prescriptive: reproducibility is an availability/throughput tradeoff a serving operator controls, not a law of the hardware.
strongest_attack: The single most damaging objection is that the thesis is trivially-true, nothing-non-obvious dressed as a discovery. To anyone who knows floating-point addition is non-associative and that GPU kernels reduce in load-dependent order, the conclusion that fixing reduction order fixes the output is definitional: of course bit-identical inputs through a bit-identical reduction schedule yield bit-identical outputs. The empirical 80/1000 result then merely confirms the tautology rather than testing a real hypothesis. Worse, the prescriptive half may be aging badly and is overclaimed from a single source: the s1 cost figures (1.6x to 2x) come from one model on one hardware and kernel snapshot and may not generalize across architectures, longer contexts, or speculative-decoding and MoE serving where batch composition interacts with routing; and the s2 verify-rollback escape hatch is asserted, not independently shown to keep amortized overhead low under adversarial or determinism-heavy workloads. If verification requires recomputation, the fast path plus verify can cost more than just running batch-invariant kernels everywhere, collapsing the headline 'you need not pay it globally' into a conditional that holds only when determinism-requiring traffic is sparse, which the thesis assumes rather than establishes.
reconciliation: The thesis survives, because the attack overstates the obviousness and the load-bearing claim is causal-prescriptive, not the floating-point lemma. The widely-held prior was the opposite of trivial: practitioners routinely attributed temp-0 nondeterminism to 'GPU floating-point being inherently unreproducible' or to uncontrollable concurrency, treating it as unfixable. The contribution is locating the real, controllable cause (batch-size-variant reduction order across specific kernels) and demonstrating it can be eliminated. That reframing flips a perceived hardware law into an engineering tradeoff, which is the non-obvious, falsifiable, and actionable core; the 80-to-1 collapse is a genuine single-variable intervention (change one thing, watch the effect vanish), not a tautology restated. The attack does land on two boundaries that must be conceded rather than papered over: the cost numbers are single-source and single-snapshot and should be framed as an existence proof of bounded cost, not a universal constant; and s2's selective determinism is conditional on determinism-requiring traffic being a minority, with verify-rollback only winning when verification is cheaper than full batch-invariant recompute. Conceding those scopes the claim without defeating it.
strengthened_argument: Temperature-0 LLM nondeterminism is an engineering choice, not a hardware law: the cause is batch-size-variant reduction order in matmul, RMSNorm, and attention kernels, and removing it makes output bit-identical (Qwen3-235B: 80 unique completions in 1000 runs, all identical with batch-invariant kernels) [s1]. This is the load-bearing, counter-to-folk-belief claim. Determinism is then a purchasable availability/throughput tradeoff with a demonstrated bounded cost on at least one production-scale model (about 2x, narrowing to 1.6x with better attention kernels), offered as an existence proof that the cost is finite and engineerable rather than a universal multiplier [s1]. Because the tax scales with how much traffic actually needs determinism, an operator can avoid paying it globally: keep a fast non-deterministic default and enforce determinism selectively via a verify-rollback loop over existing kernels, with the caveat that this wins only when determinism-requiring traffic is a minority and verification is cheaper than always-on batch-invariant recompute [s2]. Net: reproducibility at temp 0 is a knob serving operators control, and the only open questions are the magnitude of the cost across architectures and the crossover point at which selective verification beats global invariance.
reason: The argument's core claim is causal and prescriptive (the cause of temp-0 nondeterminism is controllable batch-variant reduction order, not inherent FP unreproducibility), backed by a clean single-variable intervention (80/1000 unique collapsing to all-identical) that disconfirms the prevailing folk belief, so it is neither unfalsifiable nor trivially-true. The strongest attack (trivial/obvious plus single-source overgeneralized cost) lands on cost-universality and the s2 selective-determinism conditional, but those are scopeable caveats that strengthen rather than defeat the thesis; the attack does not win, so the verdict is defensible.
